records.name: Turkey
records.current_summary:
Turkey presents real, structured danger for trans visitors — institutionalised, presidential-level hostility that has become state policy. Police profile and detain trans women for identity checks (20 were detained in Istanbul in July 2025), trans women have historically been "frequent targets of torture and ill-treatment" by police, and a trans woman attacked with a knife was herself detained (victim-criminalised). A draft law leaked in October 2025 would criminalise LGBT people — not yet passed but under active government consideration.

Transphobic attacks and Pride-event violence are documented, the Health Ministry is introducing regulations that may profile and restrict trans healthcare, and foreign visitors must carry original passports at all times — creating outing risk at the frequent transit checkpoints. If detained, trans women are placed in men's facilities with documented rights violations.

The risk is concentrated in urban trans-visible contexts (Istanbul's Beyoğlu/Tarlabaşı) rather than package-holiday tourist zones, but the institutional hostility pervades. Turkey is outside the Schengen area.
records.current_localsOnly: The Health Ministry's trans-healthcare regulations are resident-facing; the men's-facility placement of trans women concerns resident detainees.
records.current_outOfScope: General terrorism and crime advisories affect all travellers to Turkey.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025): a draft legislative package would effectively criminalise LGBT people under vague claims of protecting 'the family' and 'public morals' — framing the Erdoğan government has repeatedly used to legitimise stigmatisation; sets the reform backdrop as authoritarian drift. Key legislative-risk evidence for 2025-26.

Kaos GL (Feb 2026): the LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations in 2025 — about two-and-a-half times 2024 — dominated by detention (299 detention decisions: 256 on record, 43 off the record), plus systematic privacy attacks; frames hostility turned into state policy. Quantified annual evidence.

bianet (Aug 2025): Istanbul police detain ~20 trans women for ID checks amid profiling concerns - stopped on the street, while shopping or in cafés in Beyoğlu, held at Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released after 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks; legal experts argue GBT checks violate ECHR Article 5; one detainee: 'They didn't fine us, but they documented us. The new law hasn't even passed yet, but they're already enforcing it on us.'

Turkish Minute (26 Feb 2026): covers the Kaos GL 2025 report — hundreds of cases documented via media monitoring and civil-society complaints; six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings; transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Second reporting of the annual data.

Truth Justice Memory Center (Aug 2025): monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week — violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025; senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepened homophobia and transphobia, and discrimination against LGBTI+ people and their allies was entrenched. Event-monitoring evidence.

Kaos GL (Sept 2025): a new Health Ministry regulation risks profiling trans people — after a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular added 'gender reassignment' to official reasons for medical-board reports, hospitals were barred from the 'other' option and told to issue e-reports, with online framing contested as an 'LGBT opening'. Transition-access regulatory drift.

Kaos GL (Aug 2024): trans woman Yaşam was knifed by a 17-year-old in Bakırköy; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest — activists call the detention asymmetry evidence of a state hate policy. Concrete 2024 violence + policing-asymmetry case.

Nomad Lawyer (2026): Turkey's passport-carrying rule for foreigners — original photo ID required at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and detention warnings. Direct visitor-facing document-risk evidence.

Human Rights Watch (22 May 2008): launches the 123-page report 'We Need a Law for Liberation' from 70+ interviews over three years — documents a continuing history of beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people in Turkey. Foundational historical evidence; dated (pre-2018 legal changes).

records.name: Denmark
records.current_summary:
Denmark is a historically progressive destination. It was the first European country to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration (2014), has banned conversion therapy (2023), offers nonbinary gender markers, and has comprehensive anti-discrimination protections covering gender identity. There is no rollback movement, and Copenhagen ranks among the world's most LGBTQ+-welcoming cities.

One documented weakness: the Danish Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that a trans woman who legally changed her gender but hasn't had surgery must serve in a men's prison and be strip-searched by male staff — finding this did not violate the European Convention on Human Rights. This is the same prison-placement issue documented in France, Germany, and the UK. The Danish Institute for Human Rights also flags that police under-investigate hate crimes and are not obliged to flag hate-crime motivation at the time of reporting.

Anti-trans discourse is intensifying (debate over lowering the LGR age limit; an opinion piece by a former equality minister presenting trans people as a threat to gender equality) but has not produced rollback legislation.
records.current_localsOnly: The self-declaration LGR regime (2014, nonbinary markers) is resident-facing; the 2024 Supreme Court prison-placement ruling and the LGR-age-limit debate concern residents.
records.current_outOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.

sources.claim: Context/Thomson Reuters (25 Sep 2024): Denmark's self-ID law (gender change without medical evaluation, in force since 2014) is credited by activists with cooling the trans debate; Denmark was the first country to recognise same-sex partnerships (1989) and ranks among the world's best for LGBTQ+ rights.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex couples may marry and adopt; discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics is prohibited; trans people self-determine legal gender markers and non-binary people can choose an 'X' passport marker; Aug 2024 the government announced a plan to strengthen multi-parent (3-4 parent) families.

TV 2 Denmark (10 Sep 2024): the Supreme Court held it is not a human-rights violation for a trans inmate to serve in a men's prison department — the leading Danish authority on trans placement in custody.

Danish Institute for Human Rights LGBT+ barometer: 38% of homosexuals and bisexuals report differential treatment based on gender, sexual orientation or appearance; hate speech targeting sexual orientation, gender identity/expression or sex characteristics recurs annually.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): UN Committee Against Torture 8th periodic review found some trans people, QTIBIPOCs and migrants report denial of access to spaces and services and threats; anti-trans discourse intensified as Parliament debated lowering the legal-gender-recognition age limit; committee urged psychosocial counselling and intersex remedy.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025: in July a migrant trans woman was murdered in a hotel room in Copenhagen; 40% of LGBTI students aged 15-25 reported self-harm in the past year, two to three times their classmates' rate; Denmark signed a UN resolution against intersex discrimination (March).

WanderSafe 2026 Copenhagen guide: among the world's most LGBTQ+-welcoming cities — first country to recognise same-sex partnerships (1989), marriage 2012, gender self-declaration since 2014; Danish Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in employment/services; no conversion-therapy ban yet (bill revived Aug 2026).

F&M Global Barometers Denmark profile: gender-identity-based arbitrary arrest freedoms affirmed every year 2011-2024; workplace anti-discrimination laws have covered gender identity since 2015, with fair-housing gender-identity protection throughout the period.

HuffPost (5 Feb 2013): Guatemalan trans woman Fernanda Milan became the first transgender person granted asylum in Denmark — refused return over gender identity, citing police attacks and threats for her trans activism — an early marker of Denmark's asylum treatment of trans claimants.

records.name: Norway
records.current_summary:
Norway is very safe with strong legal protections and institutional responses, but a more acute violence context than its Nordic neighbours. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration since 2016; hate speech against trans people is criminalised (2020); anti-discrimination law covers gender identity; and the police operate a dedicated Hate Crime Unit with the security service providing annual Pride threat assessments.

The offsetting factors: a terrorist shot and killed two people at Oslo Pride in 2022 (the perpetrator, an ISIS sympathiser, was sentenced to 30 years); police-reported hate crimes against queer and trans people rose sharply in 2023 (up 18% overall, with trans-specific reports nearly doubling); an anti-gender movement is growing; and underreporting barriers are documented. The security service reports a significant decline in threats for 2025 Pride, but hate-speech and intimidation risks persist.

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.
records.current_localsOnly: The self-declaration LGR regime (2016) and the criminalised hate speech provision (2020) are resident-facing.
records.current_outOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory beyond its US travel update; general urban crime is very low.

sources.claim: Official Norwegian health-rights page (Gender Recognition Act): legal gender is determined by the individual's own perception of gender identity — self-declaration decided at the tax office — from age 16 alone, 6-16 with parents, under-6 only for documented congenital DSD; a 2017 regulation covers citizens resident abroad. For this record: the official, no-medical-intervention document-change route.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Norway: reported hate crimes rose 18% in 2023, with the largest increases in crimes motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity/expression and antisemitism; Zaniar Matapour sentenced to 30 years (the strictest penalty) for the 2022 Oslo Pride mass shooting; a drag bingo event sparked online threats; a knife attack on two people investigated as a hate crime.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (2020) covers Norway outlawing hate speech against trans people (amendment to the Penal Code).

NRK (May 2024, Norwegian): record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023, but the clearance rate fell from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped; many victims report little trust in police, and a dedicated hate-crime group encourages reporting. For this record: rising reports with a documented, quantified drop in case clearance.

UiO C-REX research blog (Sept 2024): transphobic hostility in Norway manifests mainly among political extremists and religious fundamentalists — the Nordic Resistance Movement's 2017 Kristiansand march advocated 'crushing the gay lobby', and research interviews with far-right activists frame gender diversity as 'degeneracy'. For this record: organised ideological anti-trans hostility as a movement phenomenon, not street-level risk for ordinary visitors.

UiO C-REX (June 2025), HATECYCLE study of 3,000+ survey responses from LGBTQI people: only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police — barriers include mistrust, procedural obstacles and fear of personal costs, and many who did report described dismissive treatment. For this record: official statistics undercount anti-LGBTQI hate crime by a wide margin.

OSCE/ODIHR frameworks page for Norway: hate crimes are defined as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability; any offence so motivated is recorded under the framework. For this record: the statutory definition behind Norway's hate-crime counting.

Nordisk Post (Apr 2025): Norway's Police Security Service (PST) reports a 'significant decline' in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, but warns hate speech and intimidation risks remain, especially during Pride — most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than act. For this record: current threat-level assessment from the security service.

Life in Norway resource page (updated Nov 2020): Norwegians generally hold liberal attitudes toward LGBT people; Norway was among the first countries with anti-discrimination laws; directory of national resources (FRI, Skeiv Ungdom, Transgender Association, Oslo Pride). For this record: social-climate context and the support-directory landscape.

records.name: Sweden
records.current_summary:
Sweden is very safe. A new Legal Gender Recognition Act (July 2025) simplified the procedure and separated it from surgery requirements, but it still falls short of self-determination — a medical examination and a decision by the National Board of Health and Welfare are required. Sweden was the last Nordic country to reform its 1972-era LGR law.

One documented axis-C friction: the Medley swimming-pool company's national guidelines restrict trans persons' changing-room access — lawyers say this may violate discrimination law. Brå (the crime-prevention council) reports roughly 6,700 LGBTQI-related hate-crime reports, and the government is mapping digital threats against LGBTQI individuals. There are no documented severe incidents (no tourist-rape, mob violence, or Pride-terrorism equivalent to Norway's Oslo shooting). Bathrooms as such are unrestricted, and there is no criminalisation or rollback movement.
records.current_localsOnly: The 2025 LGR Act (medical examination still required) is a resident-facing process.
records.current_outOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Library of Congress entry (April 2024) covers Sweden's parliament approving new acts on legal gender and medical procedures performed on genitalia.

TGEU report of 16 July 2025: Sweden's new Legal Gender Recognition Act came into force on 1 July 2025, simplifying the procedure but falling short of a full self-determination model, with medical barriers remaining.

Swedish-language SVT report of October 2025: swimming-pool giant Medley stops trans people from choosing changing rooms - the article explains why trans customers may no longer pick changing facilities at the chain, a direct everyday-facility access setback documented for trans visitors.

Brå (National Council for Crime Prevention) report 2024:13: supplements Swedish hate-crime statistics with a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences where police identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives - the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025): a bill would extend protection of victims of conversion practices when carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure. In November the Church of Sweden decided new priests must be willing to marry same-sex couples, passing 141 votes at the 2025 Church Council.

Open-access article in Sexuality Research and Social Policy (4 February 2016, vol 13, pp 119-129): traces LGBT policy development in Sweden's military from 1944 to 2014 - the historical record behind current service conditions.

2019 edition of the Spartacus Gay Travel Index reported by Newsweek: Canada, Portugal and Sweden tied as the most LGBT-friendly travel destinations - third-party evidence on Sweden's standing as a visitor destination.

TT/The Local, 28 January 2017: Sweden's main national board decided transgender people will no longer be classified as 'mentally ill', the depathologisation step for trans residents' diagnostic status.

records.name: Finland
records.current_summary:
Finland is very safe. A 2023 reform removed the sterilisation requirement for legal gender recognition (Finland was the last EU country to do so), but a medical statement is still required — not full self-determination. Finland issued a US travel advisory for trans citizens in March 2025.

The Police University College reports record hate-crime levels (1,808 suspected cases in 2024, up 13% since 2023 — the majority racist, but sexual orientation is among the identified motives). There are no documented severe trans-specific incidents (no tourist-rape, mob violence, or police-brutality case). Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.
records.current_localsOnly: The 2023 LGR reform (medical statement still required) is a resident-facing process.
records.current_outOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory beyond its US update; general urban crime is very low.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Finland: record 1,808 suspected hate crimes in 2025 (+13% since 2023), with sexual orientation and gender identity recurrent motives (12% of cases); Finland's first conversion-practices case prosecuted as assault (convictions in March); Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to ban conversion practices (125-49) in March, though a full ban remained pending.

Finland's Police University College (Polamk, Nov 2025): record 1,808 suspected hate-crime offenses reported in 2024 — highest figure ever recorded; defamation and assault the most common types. The sexual-orientation/gender-identity-or-expression category climbed 72 -> 68 -> 126 -> 140 -> 215 -> 241 across the six reported years. The Criminal Code has no hate-crime category, so motive is only recorded in police reports — meaning SOGI-motivated incidents are counted via reported suspicion, not charge.

The Guardian (21 Mar 2025): Finland (with Denmark) updated its US travel advice for transgender citizens after reports of border ordeals following the US 'two genders' executive order — Denmark advises trans travellers to contact the US embassy in Copenhagen before departure over document issues. Signal for the record: Finland's government publicly sides with trans travellers facing document-based refusals abroad; issued as outbound advice, not destination risk.

Investigate Europe, 'The Cruel Condition' (10 Sep 2025): Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden explicitly wrote infertility requirements into law for legal gender recognition; at least 11,000 people subjected to such conditions across the six countries investigated, Sweden first (1972, in force 40 years); the last requirement was phased out at end-June 2025 — Finland's statutory sterilisation-era requirement is history, but the legacy cohort is documented.

Yle (28 Feb 2018): Parliament approved a citizens'-initiative-inspired change to the Maternity Act recognising both women in same-sex partnerships as mothers from the moment of the child's birth — second-parent registration fixed at birth rather than via adoption.

Yle (1 Mar 2017): same-sex marriage and joint adoption became legal in Finland; the western Finland register office alone had ~41 same-sex couples scheduled to marry in the first week — the operative date for all marriage-equality claims about Finland.

Yle (19 Sep 2013): the 'Tahdon2013' citizens' initiative for same-sex marriage collected 162,000+ certified signatures — largest Finnish initiative ever, far above the 50,000 threshold forcing parliamentary consideration; organiser target had been 250,000. The process route that produced the 2017 marriage law.

records.name: South Korea
records.current_summary:
South Korea is broadly workable — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and Seoul hosts one of Asia's largest Pride parades. But the country has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law (a gap not shared by EU peers), no same-sex marriage, and a conservative society where 67% of trans youth report hearing transphobic remarks from teachers.

Institutional friction is documented: the national human rights body flags a "transgender blind spot" in hospital wards (the Health Ministry can't answer how to accommodate trans patients); school bathrooms are a documented friction point for trans teens; and among trans people assigned male at birth who served in the mandatory military, 12% experienced sexual harassment or violence (this affects Korean conscripts, not foreign visitors). No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented.

Legal gender recognition runs through the courts (surgery was historically required but courts are moving to allow changes without it). Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighborhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.
records.current_localsOnly: The court-based LGR process, the hospital-ward "blind spot," school bathroom friction, and the military-service harassment data are all resident-facing (conscription does not apply to foreign visitors).
records.current_outOfScope: Foreign-tourist taxi scams and shopping complaints rose 71% in 2024 — general, not trans-specific.

sources.claim: Seoul Central District Court, final 2 Jul 2024 (no appeal): police advising a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights; symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state, recognising the infringement.

Yonhap (8 May 2024): a court (Yeongdong) ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery to change legal sex status — five plaintiffs assigned male at birth, on hormone therapy for years; the court held demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals.

The Hankyoreh (21 Mar 2024): youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong research presented 20 Mar 2024 shows trans teens avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed — a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reports holding it in and leaving school early; researchers urged law and institutional reforms for safer school environments.

Korea Herald (28 Nov 2023): the state human rights watchdog NHRCK flagged a 'transgender blind spot in hospitalisation' — the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): civilian same-sex conduct legal but criminalised in the military under Military Criminal Act Art. 92-6, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023; legal gender recognition possible; no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity; LGBTI organisations can register.

Peer-reviewed nationwide survey (Epidemiology and Health, 27 Jun 2025): 585 transgender and non-binary young adults mapped key milestones and stigmatization across life stages — documents pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.

HRW World Report 2025, South Korea chapter (events of 2024): overall relatively positive record with free media and civil society, but persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people; chapter also covers the December 2024 martial-law crisis and assembly freedoms.

misterb&b gay travel guide to South Korea safety (July 2026): broadly positive for visitors to Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighborhoods but requiring contextual understanding - military-law criminalisation, organised conservative opposition, no national anti-discrimination law, alongside rapid social change and a landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Library of Congress entry covers the South Korean Supreme Court decision allowing a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

HRW (4 Aug 2017, 'South Korea: Supreme Court Affirms LGBT Rights'): documents LGBT registration litigation — an NGO won at Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017, with the government appealing to the Seoul High Court and Supreme Court; HRW criticises years of bureaucratic obstruction of LGBT group registration.

records.name: India
records.current_summary:
India demands real caution from trans visitors, with a complex mix of constitutional protection and real practical gaps. The Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA judgment affirmed a constitutional right to self-determined gender identity, and the 2019 Act provides third-gender recognition. But a 2026 amendment bill — passed by parliament — has been called a "huge setback" by Human Rights Watch: it removes the self-identification right and narrows the legal definition.

Police abuse is documented (a trans woman was groped by a railway-protection constable to "check gender"; TheProbe documents police atrocities), airport security discriminated against a trans student at Chennai (CISF), passport authorities have demanded unwarranted medical exams, and a new penal code removed safeguards protecting trans people from sexual violence. Enforcement is uneven — only 11 of 36 states and territories have transgender protection cells.

India has no trans-murder toll comparable to Brazil and courts are protective, but the police abuse + amendment setback + safeguard removal + enforcement gaps + airport and passport friction place it in the middle of the scale. Huge subnational variation is expected: liberal metros like Bangalore and Kerala are materially safer than conservative rural north and central states.
records.current_localsOnly: The NALSA judgment, the 2019 Act's third-gender recognition, and the 2026 amendment narrowing it are resident-facing documentation regimes; the transgender protection cells serve residents.
records.current_outOfScope: General crime (theft, scams, sexual harassment of women tourists) is a documented concern in India affecting all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: HRW (26 Mar 2026): the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill amends the 2019 law to limit legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups (hijra, kinner) and intersex individuals — removing recognition for those self-identifying as trans men, trans women or non-binary; rights activists (e.g. Akkai Padmashali) call it criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. Parliament passed it in March 2026.

BBC: India's parliament passed the controversial amendment redefining how transgender people are legally recognised, dropping self-identification amid opposition and LGBTQ-community protests; government frames it as widening welfare access and anti-trafficking protection, critics say it excludes many trans/non-binary/gender-fluid people. India has an estimated ~2 million transgender people.

Times of India (Kolkata): a transwoman alleges an RPF constable groped her at the station under the pretext of 'checking gender' — an instance of identity-document/harassment friction travellers face with railway police.
The Probe (18 Jun 2024): transgender persons arrested by the RPF in Assam recount degrading treatment in custody — victim interviews documenting police abuse against trans people during detention.

New Indian Express (16 Nov 2024): openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by CISF personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification — discrimination incident at an Indian airport checkpoint that drew outrage.

Frontline (6 Sep 2024): replacing the IPC with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence — trans people fear a rise in assaults as the new criminal code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

GOV.UK policy note (Dec 2025): India bars discrimination on grounds including sex interpreted to cover gender identity; same-sex acts decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018; no same-sex marriage or civil partnership (courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units); limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying SCC OnLine blog post (Feb 2026) covered the Allahabad High Court granting relief to a trans person asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities.

Madras High Court judgment (S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, W.P.No.7284 of 2021, 7 June 2021, Justice N. Anand Venkatesh): landmark case brought by a same-sex couple harassed by police - the court's sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation, banning conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.

freshness_all.fact: Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act in MARCH 2026: replaces self-identification with mandatory medical-board determination and requires surgical intervention

records.name: China
records.current_summary:
China demands real caution — authoritarian but not criminalising. The most directly visitor-specific finding is airport discrimination: a Thai trans YouTuber was singled out and subjected to discriminatory treatment at a Chinese airport. The most severe documented case is forced psychiatric commitment: a trans woman was held for 97 days and subjected to electroshock "conversion" therapy under family pressure (she won unprecedented compensation), showing the medical/psychiatric system can be weaponized — though this targeted a resident, not a tourist.

Under Xi Jinping, the space for LGBTQ+ organising and expression is shrinking: Pride-month social-media and film censorship, a government crackdown on LGBT NGOs (2023), a performance ban on transgender TV icon Jin Xing, and cancellation of a foreign drag queen's tour. There is no criminalisation of trans identity, no bathroom restriction law, and courts can provide some protection, but there are no anti-discrimination protections.

China is a regional gender-affirming-care hub, but the parental-consent barrier applies even to adults.
records.current_localsOnly: Legal gender recognition requires surgery and parental consent at any age — a resident-facing regime; the forced psychiatric commitment case targeted a resident; the gender-affirming-care hub status and its parental-consent barrier concern residents seeking care.
records.current_outOfScope: General state surveillance, internet censorship, and arbitrary-detention risks affect all travellers to China; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: The Thaiger (27 May 2025): Thai trans YouTuber Nisamanee 'Nut' Lertvorapong alleged Chinese immigration officials laughed at, mocked and questioned her during a family trip, posting video on Instagram with 'No one should be treated differently, no matter what their gender is.' Direct visitor-facing evidence of how a visibly trans traveller was treated at a Chinese border post.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying NYT investigation (Dec 2024) covers transgender 'conversion' practices in China.

The Guardian (21 Nov 2024): performance artist Ling'er, 28, won a record monetary payout after being subjected to electroshock 'conversion' treatment — the first time a trans person had successfully challenged such treatment in China; she said she hoped the case would help other LGBTQ+ people protect their rights.

Human Rights Watch (25 Jun 2026): around Pride month, platforms scrubbed prominent LGBT social media accounts, foreign films and events with LGBT themes — HRW reads the censorship wave as illustrating a deteriorating rights situation for LGBT people in China (deepening repression restricting expression and association).

Radio Free Asia (28 Jan 2024): the CCP's crackdown against 'foreign ideologies' has made LGBTQ+ activism 'all but extinct' on the mainland — displaying rainbow flags or accessories is no longer allowed even inside venues, and in August 2023 officials removed an LGBTQ+ anthem titled 'Rainbow'. Ongoing harassment of queer expression in public space.

Foreign Policy (Jan 2025): gender transition in China is treated as 'a family affair' — even adults need parental consent to undergo gender-affirming surgery and change their legal gender (and must prove parental death if applicable); families are forced to resolve disagreements about the procedure internally. Practical barriers to care for trans residents and long-stay visitors.

Outright International overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): China's long-standing 'don't encourage, don't oppose, don't promote' posture has grown restrictive — the Cybersecurity Law and related rules censor LGBTI content deemed to 'disrupt social order'; LGBTI organisations cannot register, legal gender recognition is unavailable, and same-sex conduct has no legal protection.

CNN (3 Jan 2025): cancellation of nationwide shows by famous transgender dancer Jin Xing led some in China to fear a wider LGBTQ+ crackdown — the case of China's most visible trans star becoming a bellwether for the tightening climate.

SWI swissinfo (20 Aug 2026): a Zurich drag artist on tour in China found the space for queer subcultures shrinking first-hand — documenting how even foreign gender-nonconforming performers meet repression while working in China.

CNN (3 Mar 2016): broadcast regulator SAPPRFT guidelines banned depictions of 'abnormal sexual behaviour', including same-sex romance, from Chinese television screens — the media-censorship baseline that has persisted and now extends to social platforms.
